binders: Inherited unknown: q : R × R → R^m, with x the spatial variable, t time, and m the number of components; no particular m is selected for the integral-law discussion. [Printed p. 1, paragraph following (1.1); printed p. 4, paragraph following (1.10).]

Flux f depends on the state q and produces the endpoint fluxes in (1.10); vector compatibility with q is implicit in that equation. Linear f(q) = Aq and nonlinear fluxes are both discussed. [Printed p. 4, opening paragraph and (1.10).]

The endpoints x_1 and x_2 are arbitrary spatial points: the source explicitly says 'for any two points.' They are fixed endpoints in the displayed time derivative; their ordering is not explicitly stipulated. [Printed p. 4, Section 1.1.1, introduction to (1.10) and its displayed bounds.]
Time t remains free in the integral identity; the passage specifies no time interval or exceptional-time quantifier. [Printed p. 4, (1.10).]
hypotheses: The discussion concerns solutions of conservation laws with the integral balance (1.10), whose components represent conserved densities. It does not assert this balance for an arbitrary discontinuous function. [Printed p. 4, Section 1.1.1, (1.10) and its explanatory paragraph; printed p. 5, Section 1.1.2, reference to shock-solutions to conservation laws.]

For the stated derivation of differential equation (1.8) from integral equation (1.10), q and f(q) must be sufficiently smooth. This qualification belongs to the derivation, not to the assertion that the integral formulation accommodates discontinuities. [Printed p. 4, Section 1.1.2, first paragraph.]

The comparison at a discontinuity assumes that the solution q has a discontinuity; no specific jump profile, speed, or left and right states are imposed in this passage. [Printed p. 5, Section 1.1.2, paragraph beginning 'At a discontinuity in q'.]
conclusions: The conservation law has the integral balance d/dt ∫_[x_1]^[x_2] q(x,t) dx = f(q(x_1,t)) − f(q(x_2,t)) for any two spatial endpoints, with left-endpoint flux minus right-endpoint flux. [Printed p. 4, (1.10).]
With q and f(q) sufficiently smooth, the differential equation identified as (1.8) can be derived from integral equation (1.10). [Printed p. 4, Section 1.1.2, first sentence.]

At a discontinuity in q, differential equation (1.8) does not hold in the classical sense, whereas integral conservation law (1.10) continues to hold and is described as more fundamental. [Printed p. 5, Section 1.1.2, second paragraph.]

Discontinuities, including shock waves, occur in relevant solutions; nonlinear conservation laws can develop them even from smooth initial data. This is a possibility claim, not an assertion that every smooth initial condition develops a discontinuity. [Printed pp. 4–5, Section 1.1.2, paragraph spanning the page break.]

The sign convention in the balance is f(q(x_1,t)) − f(q(x_2,t)); temporal change is attributed to flux past the endpoints. [Printed p. 4, (1.10) and its explanatory paragraph.]
The notation f(q) denotes the flux evaluated at the state; the smoothness phrase concerns q and f(q). [Printed p. 4, opening paragraph and Section 1.1.2, first sentence.]

The displayed law contains no source term; when the modeled quantity is not conserved because of reactions, the source says source terms must be added. [Printed p. 4, Section 1.1.1, first explanatory paragraph.]

contract_plain_english: For the one-dimensional conservation-law setting, q is a possibly vector-valued conserved density, and equation (1.10) states that its total amount between any two spatial endpoints changes by the flux at the first endpoint minus the flux at the second (printed p. 1, definition of q; printed p. 4, Section 1.1.1). If q and f(q) are sufficiently smooth, this integral balance yields the differential equation referenced as (1.8) (printed p. 4, Section 1.1.2). Relevant solutions can contain discontinuities, and nonlinear conservation laws can develop them from smooth initial data. At such a discontinuity, the differential equation does not hold classically, while the integral conservation law continues to hold for the conservation-law solution (printed pp. 4–5, Section 1.1.2). These introductory pages leave the precise regularity, temporal interpretation, and endpoint conventions for discontinuous solutions unspecified (printed p. 4, (1.10); printed p. 5, Section 1.1.2).
